# 2 Kings Chapter 23 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 243v–244v

---

**1** Then the king summoned all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem.

**2** He went up to the LORD's temple, accompanied by every man of Judah, every inhabitant of Jerusalem, the priests, the prophets, and all the people — from the least to the greatest. He read aloud to them the entire Book of the Covenant that had been found in the LORD's temple.

**3** The king took his place by the pillar and renewed the covenant in the LORD's presence — pledging to follow the LORD, to obey his commands, his decrees, and his regulations with all his heart and all his soul, and to carry out the terms of the covenant written in the book. All the people committed themselves to the covenant.

**4** Then the king ordered Hilkiah the high priest, the priests next in rank, and the temple doorkeepers to remove from the LORD's temple every object made for Baal, for Asherah, and for the heavenly bodies. He burned them outside Jerusalem in the Kidron Valley and carried their ashes to Bethel.

**5** He also got rid of the pagan priests appointed by the kings of Judah to burn incense at the shrines throughout Judah and around Jerusalem — the ones who burned incense to Baal, to the sun, moon, constellations, and all the heavenly bodies.

**6** He removed the Asherah pole from the LORD's temple, took it to the Kidron Valley, burned it there, ground it to powder, and scattered the dust over the public graveyard.

**7** He tore down the quarters of the cult prostitutes that were inside the LORD's temple, where women wove ritual hangings for the Asherah.

**8** He brought in all the priests from the towns of Judah and desecrated the pagan shrines where they had burned incense, from Geba to Beersheba. He also demolished the shrines at the city gates — including the one at the entrance to the gate of Joshua the city governor, on the left as you enter the city gate.

**9** The priests from the local shrines were not allowed to serve at the LORD's altar in Jerusalem, though they could eat unleavened bread with the other priests.

**10** He desecrated Topheth in the Valley of Ben-Hinnom so that no one could ever again sacrifice a son or daughter in the fire to Molech.

**11** He removed the horses that the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun god — stationed at the entrance to the LORD's temple near the quarters of Nathan-melech, a court official — and he burned the sun chariots.

**12** He demolished the altars the kings of Judah had built on the palace roof, near the upper room of Ahaz, and the altars Manasseh had built in the two courtyards of the LORD's temple. He smashed them to pieces and threw the rubble into the Kidron Valley.

**13** The king also desecrated the pagan shrines east of Jerusalem, south of the Mount of Corruption — the ones Solomon had built for Ashtoreth the vile goddess of Sidon, Chemosh the vile god of Moab, and Milcom the detestable god of Ammon.

**14** He smashed the sacred pillars, cut down the Asherah poles, and covered the sites with human bones.

**15** He even demolished the altar at Bethel — the shrine set up by Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had led Israel into sin. He burned the shrine, ground it to powder, and burned the Asherah pole.

**16** When Josiah looked around, he noticed tombs on the hillside. He had the bones removed from them and burned on the altar, desecrating it — fulfilling the word of the LORD spoken by the man of God who had predicted these very things.

**17** "What is that marker over there?" Josiah asked. The people of the city told him, "It marks the tomb of the man of God who came from Judah and predicted exactly what you have done to the altar at Bethel."

**18** "Leave it alone," Josiah said. "Don't disturb his bones." So they left his bones undisturbed, along with those of the prophet from Samaria.

**19** Josiah also demolished all the shrine buildings throughout the towns of Samaria that the kings of Israel had built, provoking the LORD's anger. He dealt with them exactly as he had at Bethel.

**20** He executed the pagan priests on their own altars and burned human bones on those altars. Then he returned to Jerusalem.

**21** The king gave this order to all the people: "Celebrate the Passover to the LORD your God, as prescribed in this Book of the Covenant."

**22** No Passover like this had been observed since the days of the judges who led Israel — not during the entire era of the kings of Israel and Judah.

**23** But in the eighteenth year of King Josiah, this Passover was celebrated to the LORD in Jerusalem.

**24** Josiah also got rid of the mediums, the spiritists, the household gods, the idols, and every other detestable practice in Judah and Jerusalem. He did this to fulfill the requirements of the Law written in the book that Hilkiah the priest had discovered in the LORD's temple.

**25** Never before had there been a king like Josiah, who turned to the LORD with all his heart, all his soul, and all his strength, in full obedience to the Law of Moses. And no king after him was his equal.

**26** Even so, the LORD did not turn from his fierce, burning anger against Judah, because of everything Manasseh had done to provoke him.

**27** The LORD declared, "I will banish Judah from my presence, just as I banished Israel. I will reject this city I once chose — Jerusalem — and this temple where I said my name would dwell."

**28** The rest of Josiah's reign is recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.

**29** While Josiah was king, Pharaoh Neco of Egypt marched north to the Euphrates River to assist the king of Assyria. King Josiah went out to confront him, and Neco killed him at Megiddo the moment they met.

**30** Josiah's officers brought his body back from Megiddo in a chariot and buried him in his own tomb in Jerusalem. The people of the land took Josiah's son Jehoahaz, anointed him, and made him king in his father's place.

**31** Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for three months. His mother was Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah.

**32** He did what was evil in the LORD's sight, just as his ancestors had done.

**33** Pharaoh Neco imprisoned him at Riblah in the land of Hamath to prevent him from ruling in Jerusalem, and imposed on the land a levy of one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold.

**34** Pharaoh Neco then made Josiah's son Eliakim king in place of his father and changed his name to Jehoiakim. He took Jehoahaz to Egypt, where he died.

**35** Jehoiakim paid the silver and gold to Pharaoh by taxing the people of the land. He assessed each person and collected the silver and gold from the populace to pay Pharaoh Neco.

**36** Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mother was Zebidah daughter of Pedaiah from Rumah.

**37** He did what was evil in the LORD's sight, just as his ancestors had done.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 3 — Covenant renewal:** Josiah does what no king since Moses has done: he binds the entire nation to the covenant. The language echoes the Shema — "all his heart and all his soul." But this is also the Deuteronomistic writer's setup for tragedy: the most thorough obedience imaginable will prove insufficient.

**Verses 4-20 — The great purge:** The reform catalogue is overwhelming in its detail. Josiah systematically destroys every form of syncretism: Baal worship, Asherah poles, astral cults, child sacrifice sites, cult prostitution quarters, sun chariots, Solomonic shrines to foreign gods, Jeroboam's altar at Bethel. He extends his reach into the former northern kingdom. Nothing is left standing. And yet — verse 26 will declare it all futile.

**Verse 25 — "No king like him":** The superlative echoes and contrasts with Hezekiah's commendation (18:5, "no one like him among all the kings"). Together, Hezekiah and Josiah represent the best Judah could offer. Together, they were not enough.

**Verses 26-27 — The devastating "even so":** This is the theological crisis of the book. The best king in history, fully obedient to the Shema, cannot undo what Manasseh did. The sins of the father outweigh the righteousness of the son. The reader is forced to ask: if Josiah's reform cannot save Judah, what can?

**Verse 29 — Death at Megiddo:** After two chapters of heroic reform, Josiah's death is told in a single sentence. The contrast is intentional and painful. Megiddo becomes *Armageddon* in later apocalyptic tradition.

*— PNEUMA*
